title: Counting Bits
statement: Given a number n, build a list of length n + 1 where entry i is the number of 1 bits in the binary form of i. Do it in one pass over 0..n, not by counting each number from scratch.

example.caption: For n = 5 the list is 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2. For example 5 is 101, which has two 1 bits.

idea.sentence: i has the same 1 bits as i >> 1 (itself without the last bit), plus one more if that last bit was 1, so each answer is built from an earlier one.

jargon.plain: Shift every bit one place right and drop the last one. It is the same as dividing by 2 and rounding down.
The last bit of i: 1 if i is odd, 0 if even.
Dynamic programming: answer a problem by reusing answers to smaller ones you already stored.

watch.inputHint: One argument: n, e.g. 5. Presets keep n small so every row fits.

vars.meaning: the largest number to count (the list has n + 1 entries)
bits per number, about log n

rows.name: Count each number
rows.note: Every number takes up to log n steps to count its bits.

rows.name: ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
rows.note: One lookup and one add per number. The output list itself is n + 1 cells.

rows.name: ans[i & (i − 1)] + 1
rows.note: Same idea from the other trick: removing the lowest 1 leaves a smaller number with one bit fewer.

fast.takeaway: Every answer is one step away from an earlier answer, so the whole table costs one operation per entry.

stages.title: Make the table
stages.note: A list of n + 1 zeros. ans[0] stays 0 because zero has no 1 bits.

stages.title: Look at the half
stages.note: i >> 1 is i without its last bit. It is smaller than i, so its answer is already in the table.

stages.title: Add the last bit
stages.note: ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1). The dropped bit adds 1 only if it was a 1.

edges.title: n = 0
edges.why: The list still has n + 1 = 1 entry. The loop does not run.

edges.title: n = 1
edges.why: i = 1 uses ans[0]. The base entry must already be 0.

edges.title: Power of two
edges.why: A power of two has exactly one 1 bit. Each one restarts the count at 1.

edges.title: Odd versus even
edges.why: Even numbers share the count of their half. Odd numbers add one more.

gotchas.text: In JS, + binds tighter than &. ans[i >> 1] + i & 1 means (ans[i >> 1] + i) & 1, which is silently wrong. Write ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1) with the parentheses.
new Array(n + 1) holds empty slots, not zeros. fill(0) is needed, or ans[i >> 1] is undefined and the sum becomes NaN.
Go orders & above +, so half + i&1 is fine, but keep the parentheses for the reader. make([]int, n+1) already holds zeros.
Do not call a popcount helper for each i. That works but throws away the point: the answer for i is one lookup away from an answer you already have.

recap.pattern: DP on bits: reuse the half
recap.key: ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1). The count for i is the count for i without its last bit, plus that bit.
recap.complexity: Time O(n). Space O(n) for the answer.
moves: Store it and move to i + 1
